sec.title: Background
sec.p: Small cell neuroendocrine prostate cancer (SCNC) is a lethal subset of prostate cancer with limited treatment options. Talabostat, an oral small molecule inhibitor of dipeptidyl peptidases (DPP4 and DPP 8/9) triggers the inflammasome to alert and prime immune cells, leading to induction of interleukin (IL)-18 and IL-1ß, bridging innate and adaptive immunity. Talabostat was evaluated in a phase 2 study in combination with pembrolizumab in patients with SCNC.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: Patients were required to have centrally confirmed histologic evidence of de novo or treatment-emergent SCNC and progression on ≥1 prior line of systemic therapy. Patients received pembrolizumab (200 mg intravenous every 21 days) + BXCL701 0.2 mg orally two times per day for a week, with step-up to 0.3 mg two times per day on days 8–14, and 0.3 mg two times per day on days 1–14 of subsequent cycles. The primary endpoint was the composite response rate (CRR). Biomarkers including levels of DPP 8/9 expression and association with clinical outcomes were analyzed in a post hoc fashion.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: 34 patients were enrolled, including 21 (62%) with visceral metastases. Patients had received a median of 3 prior lines of systemic treatment, including 19 (56%) and 18 (53%) of patients who received prior platinum and taxane chemotherapy, respectively. In the response evaluable subset (n=30), the CRR was 20% (95% CI 7.7% to 38.6%) and the objective response rate was 13% (95% CI 3.8% to 30.7%). The median duration of objective response was 9.0 months. All responders had tumors with low tumor mutational burden and/or microsatellite stability. The median radiographic progression-free survival was 2.1 months (95% CI 1.9 to 4.2). The median overall survival (OS) was 13.7 months (95% CI 7.0 to unevaluable) and the 12-month OS rate was 54.1% (95% CI 34.2% to 70.3%). The most frequently occurring treatment-related adverse events of any grade severity were fatigue (41%), hypotension (29%), dizziness (21%), pruritus (24%), nausea (15%), and diarrhea (15%). Baseline levels of DPP9 tumor stromal expression were associated with response.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: Talabostat plus pembrolizumab demonstrates preliminary anti-tumor activity in patients with relapsed SCNC. Further evaluation in a randomized study is warranted to assess the contribution of talabostat in this high-risk disease subset.
Keywords: Prostate Cancer, Immune Checkpoint Inhibitor, Innate, Immune modulatory, Immunotherapy

sec.title: WHAT IS ALREADY KNOWN ON THIS TOPIC

list-item.p: Small cell neuroendocrine prostate cancer is a lethal subtype of prostate cancer with limited standard of care treatment options and limited responsiveness to immune checkpoint inhibition.

Talabostat (BXCL701) is an orally administered, small molecule inhibitor of dipeptidyl peptidases (DPPs), which induces robust immune stimulation by inhibiting DPP8 and DPP9 in macrophages in the tumor microenvironment and lymph nodes.

A previously reported phase 1 study demonstrated that the combination of pembrolizumab plus talabostat in prostate cancer was safe and well tolerated using a step-up, intermittent dosing schedule administered entirely on an outpatient basis.
In this phase 2 study, the combination of pembrolizumab plus talabostat demonstrated durable responses in a subset of patients with small cell neuroendocrine prostate cancer.
In correlative analyses, DPP9 expression in the stromal microenvironment was associated with clinical response.

sec.title: HOW THIS STUDY MIGHT AFFECT RESEARCH, PRACTICE OR POLICY

list-item.p: This phase 2 study adds to the clinical rationale to develop novel immunotherapeutic approaches in small cell neuroendocrine prostate cancer including talabostat and other modulators of the immune microenvironment.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer (mCRPC) resistant to androgen signaling inhibition remains a leading cause of cancer-related death among patients in the USA and globally.1,3 Small cell neuroendocrine prostate cancer (SCNC) is a lethal variant of the disease, present in less than 1% of cases at the time of diagnosis (termed de novo SCNC), but up to 20% of all patients with mCRPC on resistance to androgen pathway inhibitors (treatment-emergent SCNC).4,7 SCNC is associated with dismal survival outcomes with a median survival of less than 12 months following platinum-based chemotherapy.5 Novel systemic treatment options are urgently needed to improve outcomes for this high-risk, lethal subset of prostate cancer. The recent development of active novel systemic therapies in small cell lung cancer, including bispecific T cell engagers8 and antibody-drug conjugates,9 has spurred further interest in the development of novel therapies for SCNC.

Prostate cancer including SCNC is considered a “cold” tumor characterized by minimal T-cell infiltrates and very limited response to single-agent programmed cell death protein-1 (PD-1) targeted therapy.10,13 Resistance to immune therapy in “cold” tumors can be driven by the absence of relevant immune cells (immune desert). Activation of innate immunity may increase sensitivity to immune checkpoint inhibitors.14 Prior studies of immune checkpoint inhibitors, including PD-1 and/or cytotoxic T-lymphocyte-associated protein 4 (CTLA-4) blockade, have demonstrated very limited activity with response rates of less than 10% in microsatellite-stable SCNC.15 16

Talabostat (BXCL701) is an orally administered, small molecule inhibitor of dipeptidyl peptidases (DPPs), including DPP4 (CD26), DPP8, and DPP9, members of the post-prolyl-cleaving protease family.17 Talabostat treatment results in robust immune stimulation by inhibiting DPP8 and DPP9 in macrophages in the tumor microenvironment (TME) and lymph nodes, which, in turn, release interleukin (IL)-1β, a potent activator of immune effector cells that release numerous other cytokines and chemokines that contribute to antitumor activity.18 19 Talabostat can induce an innate immune reaction and tumor inflammation, and preclinical studies have shown a synergistic antitumor effect on tumor growth inhibition with talabostat and anti-PD-1 combination therapy.20 21 A previously reported phase 1 study demonstrated that the combination of pembrolizumab plus talabostat in mCRPC was safe and well tolerated using a step-up, intermittent dosing schedule administered entirely on an outpatient basis.22

We conducted a phase 2a study to determine the efficacy and safety of talabostat in combination with pembrolizumab in patients with de novo or treatment-emergent SCNC. The planned target sample size for this phase 2a SCNC cohort was 28 patients (see Protocol).

sec.title: Study population
sec.p: Eligible patients had progressive, histologically confirmed de novo or treatment-emergent SCNC based on morphology by central pathology review (JH). Patients with treatment-emergent SCNC following androgen pathway inhibition were required to have a serum testosterone of <50 ng/dL during screening with ongoing androgen deprivation therapy. Measurable disease by RECIST (Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors) 1.1 criteria was required. Patients must have previously received at least one line of cytotoxic chemotherapy or be deemed unsuitable or refused chemotherapy on agreement with the study sponsor. Patients were enrolled regardless of genomic status with respect to microsatellite stability (MSS) or tumor mutational burden. Prior immune checkpoint inhibition with anti-PD-1/programmed-death ligand-1 (PD-L1) or CTLA-4 blockade was not allowed. Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status of 0–2 and adequate bone marrow and organ function was required. The complete list of inclusion and exclusion criteria is provided in the online supplemental Appendix.

sec.title: Study design and treatment schedule
sec.p: This was a multicenter, open-label, single-arm phase 2 study of talabostat in combination with pembrolizumab. Based on the prior phase 1b study results,22 pembrolizumab was administered 200 mg intravenously every 21 days, and talabostat was given orally 0.2 mg two times per day for cycle 1 days 1–7, with step-up to 0.3 mg two times per day on days 8–14, and 0.3 mg two times per day on days 1–14 of subsequent cycles 2 and beyond. All treatments were administered in an outpatient setting. Each treatment cycle was 21 days in length.

Dose interruption criteria for pembrolizumab followed standard dosing guidelines. Talabostat dose interruptions and/or reductions were permitted for grade ≥3 and intolerable grade 2 adverse events. For relative hypotension with systolic blood pressure <100 mm Hg and/or diastolic blood pressure <60 mm Hg, or symptoms of orthostasis, talabostat was held and then restarted at one lower dose level (0.2 mg two times per day).

Patients continued study treatment until radiographic progression by RECIST/Prostate Cancer Working Group 3 criteria, unequivocal clinical progression, unacceptable toxicity, or study withdrawal. Prostate-specific antigen (PSA) progression alone was not used as a criterion for treatment discontinuation.

sec.title: Safety and efficacy assessments
sec.p: Clinical and laboratory assessments were conducted on days 1, 2, 8, 14, and 15 of cycle 1, days 1, 8 and 15 of cycle 2, and on day 1 of every cycle thereafter. Serum PSA was measured at baseline and day 1 of each treatment cycle. Circulating tumor cells (CTCs) were collected and enumerated using the CellSearch assay on cycle 1 day 1 (C1D1), C2D1, C4D1, and D1 of every third cycle thereafter.23 Tumor response monitoring was performed using whole-body bone scan and cross-sectional imaging of the chest, abdomen and pelvis at baseline and every three cycles (9 weeks) thereafter. Adverse events were graded using Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (CTCAE) V.4.03.

sec.title: Correlative assays
sec.p: All correlative assays were carried out as post hoc exploratory analyses. Archival formalin-fixed paraffin embedded (FFPE) metastatic tissue was collected during Screening. To characterize the cellular and molecular landscape of the TME, the Neogenomics MultiOmyx immunofluorescence platform was applied to pretreatment evaluable FFPE tumor tissue. The archival FFPE slides were scanned into digital images and reviewed centrally by independent pathologists blinded to treatment outcomes (Neogenomics) to determine the region of interest. Each slide image was divided into up to 30 boxes each measuring 1×1 mm2. If there was an insufficient number of viable tumor cells/region-of-interest, it was not counted for analysis. The total number of biomarker-positive cells per 1×1 mm2 box were counted and cell counts/mm2 were compared between responders and non-responders via Wilcoxon rank-sum test.

Mutation profiling of baseline circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) was assessed using a next-generation sequencing panel (521-gene panel; 25,000X coverage, PGDx elio) to determine the predictive value of mutation burden or specific gene mutations. Wilcoxon rank-sum test was used to compare the tumor mutational burden between responders and non-responders.

Additional mechanism-based pharmacodynamic endpoints were evaluated by comparing pretreatment and post-treatment immune activation by multiplex serum cytokine profiling using electrochemiluminescence labels (NorthEast BioLab, MSD platform, Hamden, Connecticut, USA) measured predose and 6-hour and 24-hour post C1D1 dose. The maximal fold change from baseline was compared between responders and non-responders using Wilcoxon rank-sum test.

sec.title: Statistical considerations
sec.p: The primary study endpoint was the composite response rate, defined as one or more of the following: objective response by RECIST 1.1 criteria, CTC conversion from ≥5/7.5 mL to <5/7.5 mL, and/or ≥50% PSA decline from baseline. Secondary endpoints included the frequency and severity of adverse events as graded by CTCAE V.4.03, objective response rate, duration of objective response, PSA50 response, CTC conversion rate, radiographic progression-free survival (rPFS), overall survival (OS), and change from baseline in serum cytokine levels. Exploratory post hoc endpoints included evaluation of the association between baseline expression of markers in the tumor and associated microenvironment and clinical outcomes.

The prespecified response evaluable patient population for composite response, objective response, and PSA50 response consisted of patients enrolled who completed at least two cycles of treatment, with at least one post-baseline response assessment. All patients who received at least one dose of study treatment were included in the safety population.

The Kaplan-Meier product limit method was used to estimate the median rPFS and OS and landmark analyses at 6 and 12 months, respectively. Wilcoxon rank-sum test was used to compare biomarker-positive cell counts in archival tumor biopsies obtained from responders and non-responders. A p value of less than 0.05 was considered statistically significant. There was no adjustment for multiple comparison for these exploratory analyses.

sec.title: Study population and patient disposition
sec.p: A total of 34 patients were enrolled across 11 investigational sites, 8 in the USA and 3 in the UK, exceeding the target enrollment by 6 patients. Baseline characteristics of the enrolled patients are shown in table 1. The median age at study entry was 68 (range 54–80). 10 patients (29%) had de novo SCNC at the time of diagnosis. The median number of prior lines of systemic therapy was 3 (range 1–8), including 19 (56%) and 18 (53%) of patients who received prior platinum and taxane chemotherapy, respectively. The majority of patients had visceral organ metastases with radiographic progression of disease in the viscera at the time of study entry.

sec.p: All 34 patients discontinued treatment. 24 (71%) patients discontinued treatment due to disease progression; 4 (12%) for adverse events, 2 (6%) due to patient withdrawal, and 4 (12%) for other reasons. The median number of treatment cycles administered was 3 (range 1–30). Six patients were treated beyond initial radiographic progression which was allowed per protocol.

sec.title: Efficacy
sec.p: In the response evaluable subset of 30 patients, the composite response rate was 20% (95% CI 7.7% to 38.6%) and the confirmed objective response rate was 13% (table 2; figure 1A). The median duration of response was 9.0 months (IQR: 6.2–not reached) (figure 1B). Three out of the four patients with an objective response had received prior platinum-based chemotherapy. All patients with response had tumor genomic profiling that indicated microsatellite stable and/or low tumor mutational burden by next-generation sequencing. Objective responses were noted in target lesions including liver (n=2 lesions; one patient), lung (n=3 lesions, two patients), lymph node (n=5 lesions; one patient), and other soft tissue (n=1 lesion; one patient). CTC conversion from ≥5/7.5 mL to <5/7.5 mL blood was observed in one out of five evaluable patients (20%) (table 2). Three of six patients (50%) converted from detectable to undetectable CTCs on treatment. The PSA50 response proportion was 10% (3/30 evaluable patients).

sec.p: Of the six patients with a composite response, one (17%) responded by PSA criteria alone, three (50%) responded by objective response criteria alone, one (17%) patient had both PSA50 and CTC conversion ≥5/7.5 mL to <5/7.5 mL blood, and finally, one (17%) patient had both an objective response and PSA50 response.

With a total of 27 observed events, and median follow-up time of 23.9 months, the median rPFS was 2.1 months (95% CI 1.9 to 4.2) and the 6-month and 12-month rPFS rates were 18.1% (95% CI 6.7% to 33.9%) and 9.6% (95% CI 2.0% to 24.7%), respectively (figure 1C). With a total of 17 observed deaths, the median OS was 13.7 months (95% CI 7.0 to unevaluable) and the 6-month and 12-month OS rates were 79.5% (95% CI 59.9% to 90.1%) and 54.1% (95% CI 34.2% to 70.3%) (figure 1D).

sec.title: Safety
sec.p: 32 (94%) patients experienced a treatment-related adverse event of any grade, while 10 (29%) patients experienced at least one grade ≥3 treatment-related adverse event (table 3). The most frequently occurring treatment-related adverse events of any grade severity were fatigue (41%), hypotension (29%), dizziness (21%), pruritus (24%), nausea (15%), and diarrhea (15%). Treatment-related grade ≥3 adverse events were hypotension (n=2; 6%), edema (n=1, 3%), hyponatremia (n=1, 3%), rash (n=1, 3%), colitis (n=1, 3%), anemia (n=1, 3%), fatigue (n=1, 3%), acute renal insufficiency (n=1, 3%) and tumor lysis (n=1, 3%). Hypotension and dizziness were transient and occurred during cycle 1 in the context of step dosing and cytokine induction; the events were largely reversible with two grade 3 hypotension episodes which resolved with intravenous fluids. There were four immune-related adverse grade ≥3 events (hypotension, n=2; colitis and rash, n=1 each). Both the colitis and rash were reversible with treatment interruption and institution of corticosteroids. There were no adverse events of cytokine release syndrome (fever with or without hypotension) or immune effector cell-associated neurologic toxicity.

sec.p: Treatment discontinuation of at least one study drug due to an adverse event was required in seven patients (21%). Adverse events leading to treatment discontinuation of both study medications included acute renal injury (n=1), abdominal pain (n=1), increased liver function tests (n=1), optic neuritis (n=1), back pain (n=1), and tumor lysis (n=1). One additional patient discontinued talabostat but continued pembrolizumab due to generalized edema. Dose interruptions and reductions of talabostat due to adverse events during treatment were required in 13 (38%) and 6 (18%) of patients, respectively.

Treatment-related serious adverse events (SAEs) occurred in six patients (18%). Treatment-related SAEs included generalized edema (n=1), hypotension (n=1), orthostasis (n=1), hypothyroidism (n=1), colitis (n=1) and tumor lysis (n=1). There was one treatment-related death observed during treatment, attributable to tumor lysis. This patient presented with extensive liver metastases at study entry, and shortly after initiating study treatment was admitted with tumor lysis including elevated uric acid and acute renal failure. Patient subsequently elected to transition to hospice care and died during the hospital admission.

sec.title: Immune parameters and association with clinical response
sec.p: There were six responders and five responders with paired serum cytokine data available for analysis. There were no significant differences in the fold change from baseline between responders and non-responders. The maximum difference was observed for interferon (IFN)-gamma (15.1-fold vs 7.4-fold induction of IFN-gamma in responders vs non-responders, respectively), although this did not reach statistical significance in this small sample set (figure 2, online supplemental table 1). Increased production of the inflammasome-dependent cytokines IL-1 beta and IL-18 was also observed, rising maximally to 42-fold. Other effector cytokines including IP-10 (range 0.6–14.0 fold), CXCL9 (range 1.3–55.6 fold) and tumor necrosis factor-alpha (range 1.3–4.3 fold) were also induced postdose (online supplemental table 1).

sec.p: In an exploratory post hoc analysis of 12 evaluable FFPE specimens including TME, PD-L1 expression and immune cell infiltration were low with innate immune cells as the predominant cell type. Infiltrating CD16-positive cells, CD68-positive macrophages, and CD4+ T cells but not PD-L1 expression in the stromal microenvironment were associated with response (figure 3). There were no differences between responders and non-responders in tumor infiltrating CD4+, CD8+, or Tregs (figure 3). Baseline DPP9 expression as measured by immunofluorescence was higher in the TME of responders, with a median number of DPP9+ cells/mm2 of 23.3 (range 0–341) in the stroma and 0 (range 0–419) in the tumor bed versus 0.0 (range 0–812) and 0.0 (range 0–162) (p<0.001 and 0.112 respectively) in non-responders (figure 4).

sec.p: Among eight evaluable baseline circulating tumor DNA samples that underwent comprehensive genomic profiling using a 521-gene panel, the tumor mutational burden was low and did not differ between responders and non-responders (online supplemental figure 1). The most common individual gene with pathogenic alterations was TP53 (62.5%), consistent with prior literature.23 24

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: Treatment-emergent SCNC is detected in up to 20% of all patients with mCRPC.5 SCNC and aggressive variant prostate cancer are associated with limited treatment options and shortened survival, with median survival times following platinum-based chemotherapy of less than 12 months.5 24 Genomic and immune profiling of neuroendocrine prostate cancer demonstrates an immunosuppressive TME, with prior studies of single agent anti-PD-1 blockade with avelumab demonstrating very limited activity with a response rate of less than 10%.15

The combination of pembrolizumab plus talabostat, an immune modulator via inhibition of regulatory DPPs, demonstrates encouraging anti-tumor activity in the current study. Durable responses were observed in a subset of patients, with a median duration of response of 9 months, in a heavily pretreated population the majority of whom had received prior platinum-based chemotherapy. There was no preselection of patients based on genomic status, with all objective responses observed in tumors that were microsatellite stable and/or demonstrated low tumor mutational burden. It is possible that talabostat is priming an immune response to augment response greater than what would be observed with checkpoint inhibition alone, however randomized trials are needed to further evaluate this hypothesis.

In a post hoc exploratory analysis, baseline expression of the drug target, DPP9, in the stroma was associated with response. DPP9 expression is readily characterized using a multiplex immunofluorescence platform applied to archival FFPE tissues and has also demonstrated predictive utility with talabostat in other malignancies including acute myeloid leukemia,25 underscoring its potential for prospective validation as a predictive biomarker in future studies of talabostat and other agents targeting the DPP family.

The potential for an immune priming effect of talabostat is potentially also supported by the observation of upregulation of serum cytokines relevant to its mechanism of action, including IL-1 beta, IL-18, and IFN-gamma. Though the limited sample size and absence of randomized trial design precluded definitive assessment, upregulation of serum cytokines, in particular IFN-gamma, appeared to be associated with clinical response. Immune cell infiltrates in the tumor stroma, in particular CD16+ innate immune cells, CD68+ macrophages, but not PD-L1 expression nor baseline tumor infiltrating CD8+T cells, were associated with clinical response. The low tumor mutational burden and MSS status coupled with the low baseline T cell and PD-L1 expression signatures suggest a possible pharmacological mechanism where talabostat modulates an otherwise cold immune checkpoint inhibitor-refractory TME into a permissive phenotype that promotes responsiveness to PD-1 blockade. A randomized trial of pembrolizumab with or without talabostat will be needed to further evaluate this hypothesis.

The treatment combination was generally well tolerated without an apparent increase in immune-related adverse effects compared with the frequency expected with anti-PD-1 immune checkpoint inhibition as a monotherapy. The risks of transient hypotension and orthostasis, related to initiation of dosing with cytokine release in cycle 1, were partially mitigated with the use of step dosing in week 1 and frequent ambulatory blood pressure monitoring with dose interruptions permitted. Notably, there were no events of high-grade cytokine release syndrome, and a fully outpatient dosing schedule was feasible, which is distinct from other immune modulatory approaches currently in clinical evaluation in advanced prostate cancer including bispecific T cell engagers.26

There were several limitations of this study. A randomized study will be important to distinguish the individual contributions of talabostat and pembrolizumab to the antitumor activity observed with the combination, given the single arm design of the current study and relative dearth of robust historical control data with immune checkpoint inhibition monotherapy in SCNC. Comparison with historical control data is further limited by variability in the definition of SCNC, heterogeneity of prior therapy preceding study enrollment, and differences in response definition (eg, objective vs composite response). In addition, though the efficacy evaluable population was prespecified to include only those patients who completed at least two cycles of treatment with at least one post-treatment initiation efficacy assessment, this excluded 12% of patients without an observed response on study. Additionally, the composite response rate used CTC conversion, the utility of which was limited by only five patients with baseline CTC counts >7.5/5 mL. Finally, some patients with SCNC have very low serum PSA levels and inclusion of PSA response may not be reflective of underlying tumor response. Only one of the six patients with composite response in the current study met criteria by PSA alone. Potentially utilization of molecular response data by evaluation of changes in circulating tumor DNA fraction may be a more robust means to assess for clinical activity, especially in the SCNC setting where there are frequent genomic alterations in TP53, RB1, and/or PTEN.5 7

There was a limited number of evaluable samples for the correlative analyses including ctDNA and evaluable tumor tissue, which may have precluded the ability to identify additional predictive biomarkers of response. Furthermore, on-treatment tumor biopsies were not collected, which will be important to assess the impact of the treatment combination on the TME.

Patient identification for robust clinical trial enrollment in SCNC requires morphologic confirmation of small cell neuroendocrine histology, frequently of metastatic castration-resistant tumor tissue, using standardized central pathology review and consensus criteria.27 The availability of evaluable tumor tissue may be difficult to obtain in patients with bone-predominant SCNC however it is included in standard treatment guidelines,28 and careful site selection is important for successful accrual to trials enrolling patients with SCNC. Whether non-invasive means to identify SCNC are feasible requires further prospective evaluation.29

In summary, there was preliminarily encouraging activity with durable responses noted in a subset of patients particularly those with tumors harboring DPP9 overexpression in the TME. The observed median survival compares favorably with expected outcomes following platinum-based chemotherapy in the SCNC population, where median survival is typically less than 1 year.5 Further evaluation is warranted in both SCNC as well as in other high-grade neuroendocrine carcinomas including small cell lung cancer and GI neuroendocrine neoplasms, as well as in combination with DLL3-targeting T cell engagers8 and other systemic therapies, given the high unmet need in these patient populations.
